subject: Agriculture
title: Africa Left Behind
description: A quick, practical guide to Africa Left Behind.

hook.text: The Green Revolution transformed Asia. In Africa, it barely happened. Why?

buildup.text: Africa's crops—sorghum, millet, cassava—weren't the focus of international breeding programs that targeted wheat and rice.

discovery.text: Africa lacks irrigation infrastructure. Only 5% of cropland is irrigated, versus 40% in Asia.

twist.text: Diverse soils, climates, and fragmented markets meant no single solution could spread continent-wide.

climax.text: Yields in sub-Saharan Africa remain among the world's lowest. The hunger challenge has shifted to this continent.

punchline.text: The revolution fed Asia. Africa is still waiting.

quiz.question: Why did the Green Revolution largely bypass Africa?
options: Africa's crops, soils, and lack of irrigation didn't fit the model
Seeds couldn't grow in tropical heat

details.summary: Sub-Saharan Africa largely missed the Green Revolution due to its diverse farming systems, lack of irrigation infrastructure, limited road networks, and varieties that were not adapted to African conditions.
details.whyItMatters: Africa's cereal yields remain only one-third of the global average. With the continent's population expected to double by 2050, closing the yield gap is the single most important challenge in global food security.
takeaways: African cereal yields average 1.5 tons per hectare versus 4+ tons globally
The Green Revolution's wheat and rice focus didn't match Africa's millet, sorghum, and cassava diets
AGRA and CGIAR are leading efforts to develop African-adapted high-yield varieties

faq.question: Why did the Green Revolution bypass sub-Saharan Africa?
faq.answer: Africa's staple crops (millet, sorghum, cassava, yams) received little breeding investment. Most African farming is rain-fed without irrigation. Poor roads made fertilizer delivery expensive. Diverse agroecological zones meant no single variety could work broadly.

faq.question: What is being done to bring a Green Revolution to Africa?
faq.answer: The Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA) develops improved varieties of African staple crops. CGIAR centers breed drought-tolerant maize and disease-resistant cassava. Mobile banking and digital extension are overcoming infrastructure gaps.
